utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning. The next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: The next witness is Jon Sterenberg, an archaeologist with ICMP. Mr. Stamp is the one who is leading this witness. He will be here. We're sorry for the inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have the witness in court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you stand, please, Mr. Sterenberg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sterenberg. Can you just start by telling us your name and your occupation presently?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Jon Sterenberg. I'm the current head of excavation and examination at the International Commission on Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By profession, what are you?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: By profession I'm an archaeologist, but I've been involved with the forensic recovery since 1997 in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And by forensic recovery, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Generally, the location and excavation of human remains from mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, between the years 2001 and 2002, were exhumations of mass graves conducted at Batajnica in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. Between 2001 and 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also in that period of time, were exhumation of mass graves found at a place called lake Perucac in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That is also correct in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also at a place called Derventa canyon?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Also correct in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And were those excavations observed by the ICMP? Did the ICMP participate in the excavations of these mass graves?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes. In 2001, ICMP had a forensic monitor at the sites at Derventa canyon and Petrovo Selo, and also in 2001, at a small site in Batajnica BA01 and, again, in 2001, another site also at Batajnica BA02 . ICMP also had a full forensic team on the ground in 2002 to finish Batajnica 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in respect to the work of the ICMP in these excavations, did you prepare a report summarising the work and observations made by the ICMP personnel at these various locations?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes. A report was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2476.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see the cover page there of the report?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes. I see that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's page 1 on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 48 -- or perhaps not. May I just indicate to the Court that page 48, 49, and 50 of the -- I think 48 to 50 -- 54 comprise the curriculum vitae of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in September this year, did you give a statement to the OTP, making certain corrections to your report and explaining certain aspects of your report?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: I did. I made that at the ICTY office in Sarajevo, and I have since made just two small minor corrections to the report that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I'll get to those corrections. I want to show you your statement first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have on the ELMO Exhibit P2557. Sorry, not on the ELMO, on e-court. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the exhibit you actually want?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it's the statement. It's 2475.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 2475, I beg your pardon. Could we just scroll to the last page of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document that we've just scrolled through, Mr. Sterenberg, is that the statement you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes, that's the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back briefly to the report. Perhaps we could start first with the corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the report, could we have a look at paragraph 3, and that is P2476. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we get to page 10 in e-court. Yes, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, the first sentence thereof reads: "A third site, Batajnica 3 (BAO3), was excavated on the 23rd and 26th July 2002, also on the firing range slightly north of BA02." Is there something you want to correct there?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Just a slight correction on the dates. My notebooks indicate that it was the 20th of June and the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 20th of June to the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we're on that page, can you have a look at paragraph 7. It says: "In the following report, archaeological features and contexts defined during field-work, and subsequently in post excavation analysis, are discussed within the chronological event system defined in the first instance through stratographic relationships or likely spatially associations." Can you explain briefly, if you can, what that sentence means, just elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: The role of the archaeologist on site is to try and identify features that are spatially equivalent or slightly different to each other. What we do is actually use the evidence that we find during recovery to try and put the sites in order. It's a well established archaeological technique that's used throughout the world at the present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a expression in that the paragraph: "The report presents the excavated features in order of excavation and examines the potential of the associated forensic artefacts." What do you mean by examines the potential?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for the sort of potential that we were looking at in respect of these sites, was the various possible separate body deposits that we recovered from each of the graves. So the features were actually the mass graves themselves, the deposits within the human remains, and the associated artefacts were related to those remains, but also linked to vehicles or whatever might have brought those remains to the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this the potential for identifying the persons in the grave, or is it potential for demonstrating the circumstances in which the graves were created or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is it all of these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's all of that. It's related to presumptive identifications that were recovered during the actual excavation. As I said, the remains themselves, they also have evidence within them that might link them to a certain location. So it's all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's one of these adjectives that nowadays has taken on the role of a noun.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to page 12 at paragraph 12. Sorry. I meant page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have here a site plan of Batajnica showing the location and the basic arrangement of the mass graves. And to the bottom right-hand corner there is a scale; and to the top of the -- this diagram, this outline, you will see abutting on the broken line. And the broken line is the site outline or something marked 300 metre target trench. Could you just explain what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yeah. The sites that are shown on this map, they were all located at the northern end of the 300 metre firing range, which is actually a firing range; and at various points along the train, there are concrete trenches that are used for pop-up targets for practice. The concrete trench si marked in this map as the 300-mark target trench. There was another one at 200 metres, but that hasn't been mapped on to these -- on to this plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just move to the next page, please. Your Honour, to the extent that good photographs -- photographs in which one can see features might be needed, I'm not sure that these are ideal. However, we could upon request provide hard copies of colour photographs, at least of those pages where there are photographs. I'm in the hands of the Court on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, subject to what emerges in the course of examination and ultimately cross-examination, it doesn't seem to me that the photographs are an essential part of this report for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 12, you indicate: "An initial visit was made by the ICMP at the beginning of June 2002 before invasive work was undertaken." Is that June 2002 or 2001?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That would be June 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid I -- can you explain -- the Batajnica sites were --

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: There was -- yeah. Sorry. There was a break between the Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2 excavations. ICMP then returned in June 2002 to undertake the next series of excavations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Here we're referring to Batajnica 2?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: No. Here we're referring to Batajnica 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move, I have a question for you in relation to paragraph 13, when you say: "Following the completion of work on Batajnica 2, the site had been turned over to the SAJ who had conducted ballistic experiments and live fire exercises." Now, when you say the "completion of work," are you talking about work of burial, or are you talking about work of examining the mass grave site that you were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This refers to the completion of the excavation and recovery of remains from Batajnica 2, so following that the site was backfilled, leveled, and returned back to the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that at a stage after you were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should probably just point out that I wasn't strictly involved in the excavation recovery of Batajnica 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. No, I mean the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it after they were involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's after their involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what is the point you're making in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's just to try and show that at some stage between excavation 1 -- of Batajnica 1 and 2, there was a slight break where the range had been returned back to its -- let's call it a live fire range. So, consequently, when we arrived in June 2002, there was a lot of ballistic material already lying on the ground. And what we didn't want to do is actually try and confuse that evidence with the material that we might find inside the graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, that's -- I remain confused, because the way this paragraph is written: "Following the completion of work ... the site had been turned over to the SAJ." I thought you indicated me a moment ago that that was following the excavation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you're suggesting what I thought it meant, that it was following the burial and before the excavation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I can understand that. I think that is probably just a very badly written paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you now have to clarify it for us. Are you saying that after you had done all your excavation work, its use was resumed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a live fire range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- as a fire range.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's the use of this paragraph if all these casings arrive after your work's all done, what's the point of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's just to indicate that the site had been used as a live fire range before ICMP returned in June 2002 to carry on the excavation of BA3 up to 8, and the whole surface was just covered in ballistic material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. So the relevance of this is on to the other sites, 3 and onwards sites, and it's irrelevant as far as Batajnica 2 is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. As I said, that's badly written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at the next page. And could we go ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 15, the first paragraph reads: "It was reported to the ICMP that 22 truckloads (i.e. Approximately 220 cubic metres) of soil had been brought on to the site to remodel the surface of the area, presumably following the backfilling of the graves, in the particular the north-east end of the range where the activity of grave construction had altered the ground water table." Is there anything there that you would like to correct?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Again, the actual report that the material had been brought to the site. On checking my original notebooks, I think that I might have made a slight mistake with the amount of trucks that brought the material to the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know the amount of trucks or what was reported to you? Do you have an accurate recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So in other words, you don't know how many truckloads from the report?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I think it was either 22 truckloads or 220 truckloads. I'm afraid that my notes are slightly ambiguous at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were the archaeologists who were there not able to estimate whether large quantity of material had been brought on to the site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The archaeologists did actually observe that a lot of material had been brought to the site, but it was trying to gauge how many truckloads had brought them in the first instance to conceal the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at the -- well, it's just like to read the rest of the paragraph and get back to His Honour's question. The paragraph continues from where I left off last: "The soil was also to be used to combat the problem of the area where the ground had now taken on a swampy appearance. Finally, it was used to create a false horizon that sloped from the original ground surface, approximately the centreline (north/south) of the site and extended towards the eastern berm." Firstly, can you say what was the approximate depth of the soil that covered the area?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: The approximate depth was very thin towards the centre line, and then it -- as a sort of wedge shape, it went down a metre at the eastern end. And it seemed to cover the area of about 45 metres by 50 metres. So it's difficult to gauge exactly how many tons of material was placed over the top of the graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us, again, the area that you said was covered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's approximately 45 metres by -- just bear with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In giving that answer, you're referring to the outline that you drew in the report?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: My apologies. It's 25 metres by 45 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said 45 just now, earlier.

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: If you -- sorry. If you look at figure 2, the plan outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: The scale -- the soil was deposited roughly to the north edge of BA07, which is about 25 metres from the eastern berm, and approximately about 45 metres length.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. At paragraph 16, and this is page -- this is the same page that we were at in e-court and the preceding paragraphs, you discuss the methodology employed by the ICMP at the various excavation sites and also the system of making records. Was this system standardised by the ICMP in terms of excavations?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Every site that ICMP goes to follow a standard process. This is similar for any site, be it in BiH, Serbia, or anywhere else in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in respect to those sites that you didn't personally participate in, you examined and used the standardised data recorded by the ICMP personnel?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraph 24, and that is page 15, you say: "It is difficult to generally comment on the state of the remains at Batajnica due to several preburial taphonomic features," and you continued, thereafter, to discuss the condition of the bodies. Could you just tell us what the feature taphonomic factors?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: The taphonomic factors that relate to the human remains are actually what the condition of the soil, water, and oxygen levels present in the ground, their effect on the human remains when they're buried. So, for instance, you can have one set of remains that the oxygen and the water, et cetera, is completely skeletonised and two to three feet away you might have a body that's completely intact. So the taphonomic variables are completely different throughout the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on to paragraph 44 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that in paragraph 25, you deal with the process -- what you describe as the process of autopsy. That's at the top of page 15 of the report. What was the nature of these autopsies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the autopsies were all undertaken by the pathologist for the forensic institute of Belgrade. They were all undertaken at the site. ICMP's role was actually to just monitor the autopsies. We had no input in the actual data that was being put into the computers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did they involve dissection of the bodies or simply examination of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was partly both, actually. As I said, some of the remains that were skeletonised, they just became the property of the anthropologists who were also from the Belgrade institutes. The identity of the bodies, the ones that were still fleshed, they had a full autopsy undertaken on each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move on to paragraph 44, and that is page 21 -- 22. And this paragraph relates to the excavation at Batajnica 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you say: "12 separate deposits of human remains were recovered." And below that there is a picture of the elongated grave after it was fully excavated. What do you mean by "12 separate deposits of human remains?"

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: What we're -- as archaeologists, what we're trying to do is actually separate deposits of remains within each site. As we found in Bosnia, we do find separate material coming from various sites being deposited in one grave. One of the things that we tried to do, especially with Batajnica 5, is to identify if there was -- if there were separate deposits that possibly came from different areas in Kosovo. So the deposits themselves were actually identified before we could recover them. So very careful, cleaning, looking for identifying factors that might actually link them to separate areas. At the end of the excavation at Batajnica 5, we had identified 12 very unique and separate deposits of remains all coming to that one location for burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at paragraph 50 on the next page in respect to Batajnica 7, you say the same thing: "Five separate deposits were recovered" --

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would that also apply there, too?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes. It's a method of trying to identify separate deposits in the grave for each.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just indicate to the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. At the end of paragraph 50, you say that samples of the soil types were gathered and you recommended further analysis. Do you know if anything came of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know whether they were analysed any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate to the Court that the document speaks for itself, but from pages 28 forward the document deals with the excavations at Petrovo Selo and Derventa canyon. But there is nothing in that area that I wish to -- that I think I need to ask about in chief. The report is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you briefly to describe an outline - I know you're a forensic anthropologist - the system the ICMP uses in respect to identification of human remains.

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Well, ICMP has a -- quite a large forensic science division, which incorporates three separate areas of expertise. One is excavation and examination, which is basic identification of sites, recovery of human remains, and the processing of those remains at facilities. The second area is the coordination division, which actually looks for and collects ante mortem data, but also at the same time collects blood samples that are used to support the third area, which is DNA identification, where the blood samples are matched against the DNA profiles. All three of the divisions worked together towards identifying remains from any sites in any region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The blood samples which are matched -- let's call them reference samples, from whom are they collected?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Those samples are recovered or taken from surviving family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is family members of persons reported missing?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Family members of persons reported missing, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And -- well, obviously, but I say it again. You say they are matched against the DNA profiles, you mean the DNA profiles of the human remains that are found at various sites?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's only in relation to one of these excavations that you actually mention in the report taking DNA samples. Were DNA samples taken in relation to all these recoveries; Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and the canyon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Samples were taken. I only mentioned the one site, because that is the one set of autopsies that I monitored myself. I gather from other ICMP monitors on the ground that DNA samples were taken regularly from every set of remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at annex 1 of the report, annex 1A, and that's at page 40. And this is a document entitled ICMP fact sheet which gives an overview and mandate of the work of the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It says in respect to mandate: "ICMP endeavours to secure the cooperation of governments and other authorities in locating and identifying persons missing as a result of armed conflicts, other hostilities, or violations of human rights and to assist them in doing so. ICMP also supports the work of other organisations in their efforts, encourages public involvement in its activities, and contributes to the development of appropriate expressions of commemoration and tribute to the missing." And it goes on: "ICMP is an international organisation that was created in 1996, following the G-7 Summit to address the issues of persons missing as a result of different conflicts relevant to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia, Serbia, and Montenegro from 1991 to 1995. "Following the conflict in Kosovo and the crisis in the former Yugoslavia, Republic of Macedonia, ICMP expanded its operations to address missing person cases from these areas." The work of the ICMP, the standardised work of the ICMP has been ongoing since when? How long has the ICMP been involved in excavating mass graves and making DNA matches between family of survivors and remains found in these mass graves?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Well, ICMP has been involved in the process since 1997 in BiH. It's been recovering remains, working in conjunction with the local commissions and court authorities in BiH since that time. In 2002, ICMP actually brought in archaeologists as a sort of additional expertise area, and that is where sites have been excavated as well as can be expected given an international standard. That process continues to this day. ICMP also has three facilities that are based in BiH where a lot of the recovered remains are actually handed over and worked on by international and national anthropologists. It's at that point that the DNA samples were actually taken. They're then processed by the ICMP laboratories in Sarajevo, and then a physical match is actually brought together at the very end of the process between the pathologist, the anthropologist who actually undertook the work, and with the DNA profile to try and give a hundred percent positive identification to that set of remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to elaborate a little bit further on the physical match is actually brought together at the very end of the process between the pathologist, the anthropologist, and what the DNA profile was. What is the role of the various parties in making this 100 percent identification in particular?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Well, the pathologist -- ICMP itself does not really have court-appointed pathologists who can actually give closure to all the cases. So ICMP employs a chief forensic pathologist, who is half working for the local court and half working for ICMP. He has legal authority to close cases at the end of an identification. His role is to look for any identifying factors or elements in the body that might indicate trauma, i.e., gun-shot injury, signs of severe beatings, or anything like that that might link them to -- link those set of remains to a location where they were last seen, where that individual might have been last seen. The anthropologist is actually there to give the expertise based on the skeletal knowledge that they have, which is also to backup the pathologist's observations and to assist him in doing a complete skeletal inventory of the remains. Obviously, that's quite important for work that we do in BiH, because ICMP is involved in excavating large amounts of secondary material. So we need to be very careful about what we're recording so that we know that one individual may not be complete, and we might have to try and locate other parts of that individual in secondary sites. As I mentioned before, the DNA match gives an indication of the person that was -- that the profile matches; and that together with the ante mortem, if any exists, can finally look at the skeletal assemblage and age that and put it all together so that it could be that one individual. So if we have ante mortem data that states that a person has fractured a femur or something, that will actually show in the anthropology and the pathology. And it's an identifying factor when all three areas were brought back together; that allows the court pathologist to issue the certificate of death and that can be signed off and the remains can be sent back to the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does the court pathologist -- or could I just ask. Do the artefacts play a role, the artefacts that might be found on these bodies or in these graves, do they play a role in analysis?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: They definitely play a role in the process of -- as I said, trying to identify what happened to that individual. So items such as blindfolds, ligatures, they're all taken into account during the autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The process you've just described involving your own chief forensic pathologist, was that followed in relation to these excavations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was slightly different with the Batajnica material, because the court-appointed pathologists were there from the Forensic Institute of Belgrade. So they undertook all those areas that ICMP would generally do in Bosnia. They undertook all of those and so ICMP os role was strictly to monitor what their process was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what about at Petrovo Selo and Derventa canyon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a similar process. Serbian pathologists, anthropologists, with an ICMP monitor outside to make notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's the relevance of this evidence in this case, Mr. Stamp, this evidence about the methodology if it didn't apply to these excavations?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has just told us that what he's described as the Bosnia experience, as I gather it, the practice that's followed in Bosnia, not the practice that's followed in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a similar process between the two countries. It's just that ICMP's is slightly different because the system is -- let's say it's all in place at the facility. With the remains that were dealt with at Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Derventa canyon, all the remains were actually examined at the site under a tented accommodation. So it's a similar system but just in two different areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who has ultimately, though, done the identification insofar as that was possible in relation to the bodies recovered in these three areas that you're covering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those would have been done by the forensic pathologist from the Institute of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And those identifications would have been done in conjunction with the ICMP; with the DNA matches, also the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. They would have used the DNA results from ICMP to actually backup their own data that they were finding on site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I wish to remove a confusion. In the case of Batajnica, we learned that this was done because of a judicial order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But I think that the witness stated that in the rest of the cases, you don't recall -- you didn't need this. The organisation for which you work itself initiated it. So where did they get the mandate from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I might have caused a bit of confusion there. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: In case of this -- these sites, which you are mentioning, there were the judicial orders and you coordinated with the local persons to help them out. That's okay. But you said that in other -- in other sites, this was not the case because it was different. You did it on your own, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's the confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I caused a bit of confusion there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your report makes it clear the cases where there are judicial orders. It's perfectly clear from the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All judicial orders are just fitted in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, shall I try and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I'm not clear about is the extent to which your organisation is actually involved in this case in identifying the remains.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the Batajnica cases?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Derventa canyon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. ICMP is involved from the excavation and the recovery level, but also assisting with the DNA analysis part of the operation. So the DNA is then handed back to the Serbian authorities, the court, and the forensic pathologists to finish off their own identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe I could take you through this step by step. The ICMP, you said something about assisting in the DNA. Does the ICMP itself undertook and does the DNA analysis to make the matches?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: It does, yes. But the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So once the -- so the identification job of the forensic pathologist, I take it from what you have said, is in relation to identifying and putting together the body parts so that it can be returned to the relatives?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes. It's all one process, really. It's just divided, but it all falls under the local jurisdiction of the court. They obviously have to issue an order for exhumation or excavation or autopsy. ICMP's role in the Batajnica cases was to undertake the excavation and recovery and provide the DNA for the local court authorities to finish off identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does that mean the DNA from the surviving relatives of the potential victims in the graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, who -- what witness is going to be here to identify the ones which have been identified for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I intend to show him some of the -- the DNA results and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This isn't in the report we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. No, it's not. I was getting to that. Now, these DNA reports, he can't testify about those DNA -- the DNA methodology itself. They are the subject of discussions with the Defence, because it is the Prosecution's -- I should hope that these are material that can be agreed upon. Otherwise, we will call the DNA expert from the ICMP to explain the DNA procedures to get the match results. So this witness merely introduces these reports. I should -- we had hoped that there would have been an agreement in respect to the reports before now, but there have been problems in respect to finding times when we could all convene to meet. But if necessary, there will be a DNA expert who can explain the procedures in making the identifications employed by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, the ICMP can match the DNA profiles from the bones -- from the bone specimens taken from the exhumed body parts to the DNA profiles taken from the relatives of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the forensic pathologists, whoever you're working with, will be -- will take part in this identification by putting together the body or the body parts to be sent to the families in the respective countries, in Kosovo in this instance?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And without us going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate to the Court that the annex 4 is the grant agreement between the Coordination Centre to Kosovo and Metohija and the Government of Serbia in respect to the ICMP's -- this is page 56, in respect to the ICMP's jurisdiction to participate in these excavations in Serbia and the resulting return of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look quickly at --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could it be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Exhibit P02559. You recently had a look at this document, I think, a couple days ago. And is that the -- is that a report explaining the procedure? Is it the DNA procedures employed by the ICMP in making identifications?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes, that looks correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you see it's -- the document is signed by the resident DNA expert at the ICMP Director of Forensic Sciences is Dr. Parsons, and also by the Director-General of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we also have a look at P02559.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the document you've just had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we had 2557. Could we bring up 2557 then. P2557.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document, therefore, is the methodology report of the ICMP in respect to its DNA analyses for remains found in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other one that we looked at earlier looked like the results of the comparison, rather than the methodology I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed that is correct, Your Honour. Could we have a look at page 17 of this document, or the last page. It's the page after that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, you see that the methodology report is signed by the competent ICMP personnel?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, lastly, I'd like to show you Exhibit P2558. You also had a look at this document over the last couple of days. Is that also a document containing DNA match analyses by the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should indicate that the results that is P02559 are the results in respect of those matches of mortar remains found in Serbia to the blood reference samples from surviving family members. The last document that's P2558 is results in respect to mortar remains, matches of mortar remains found in both Serbia and in excavations in Kosovo to the families of surviving family members. So it includes the first but it is wider.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Sterenberg, although you have not participated -- well, let me not -- does it -- did the ICMP also participate in exhumations of graves in Kosovo itself?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the -- well, did the -- UNMIK, the United Nations Mission in Kosovo, did they send to the ICMP for examination the DNA -- well, specimen samples taken from the remains of the persons exhumed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the ICMP performed DNA match analysis on those --

utterances.speaker: JON STERENBERG
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- samples? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know the witness cannot testify about the DNA. As I indicated if we do need to, we will -- or seek leave to bring the appropriate experts. I -- just to be absolutely clear, the first set of matches only relate to those bodies exhumed at Batajnica, Derventa canyon, and Lake Perucac in Serbia. The second set of matches relate to DNA matches not only of those bodies, but also Kosovo-wide. Insofar as they relate to the case, it would be for the Prosecution to extract from the exhibit the relevant material to present to the Court in -- at the appropriate time. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify a couple of matters for me. Batajnica 1 and 3 are not the subject of this report; they are just referred to in passing in this report. Now, do we already have information on both of these sites?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Batajnica 1, we tendered the report, and the report is also referred to as approval in this report -- particular report of a forensic anthropologist whose name is Mr. Starovic. He is referred to in this report, at page 5 of his report, as the archaeological team member. He prepared a report which was reviewed by Mr. Sterenberg, and that report was submitted earlier when Professor Dunjic came to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about Batajnica 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A report in respect to Batajnica 3 has not been tendered because of the paucity of relevant bodies from that site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, my other question is: The paragraph numbers in this report are not sequential. They don't -- you don't -- you can jump paragraphs. Let me -- it may be only one area of the report. Yes. If you go to, for example, paragraph 51 if you can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There and I see in more than one place, there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you have that, Mr. Sterenberg, you will see that paragraph 51 is followed by 54, which is followed by 57, which is followed by 60. Is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, actually, the report I have doesn't jump, it goes 50, 51, 52, 53 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The report that I have here doesn't have those mistakes in it. So I'm not sure where they've come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll see on the screen the one we have. Is that different from the one you've got in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the same report. It's just the numbers are different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure why that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to make sure we're awake on a Monday morning, probably. Look forward to stern cross-examination on that point, Mr. Sterenberg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything further, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, we live in hope that the situation has changed over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there likely to be real issues for cross-examination in relation to this witness, or is it possible he won't be required to return?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I really think it's premature to say that until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic may have something to offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the main point is we received quite a large number of documents within the past I think it was week and a half, two weeks, which still have not been completely gone through by the various Defence teams. So, you know, the old adage in my jurisdiction is anything is always possible. But whether or not it's going to be likely or not, we really can't say without going through all the material and seeing what we have there and a corpus to deal with and then make that assessment. But we will endeavour to make that assessment and advise Your Honours as soon as is possible as soon as that material has been assimilated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we should set some sort of time-scale here for your response on this. Should we make it the 16th of January when we return? No objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're okay with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your position should be made clear on the 16th of January, or before if you can file something all the better. Mr. Sterenberg, the problem here relates to confidentiality which prevented earlier disclosure of material; and as a result, material has been given to the Defence fairly recently. They are not in a position to say whether they want to ask you questions and what these might be, and the Trial Chamber decided to give them time to complete that exercise. So if there are issues in relation to your evidence and your report, you are going to have to return. But as far as today is concerned, that brings your evidence to an end. We are extremely grateful to both you and the ICMP for the assistance they are giving to the Tribunal; and for the moment -- well, I convey these thanks to you and also convey them to the organisation, in case we don't see you again. But we may of course have to see you again to complete the evidence. For the moment that brings your evidence to an end and you're now free to leave the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, my apologies I should have asked that the last exhibit be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the -- you mean, 2557, 8, and 9?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Including the methodology report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are areas in that report that involve areas of technology --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know there are also reasons for it being confidential that are not necessarily technological. We have no difficulty with these being under seal at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe, though, that the results in respect to Serbia, that is 2559, perhaps can be -- perhaps the ICMP may waive the situation because those bodies were returned -- my understanding is those bodies were returned to the family members already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to see where the basis for confidential is; but in case there is something, you should double-check and notify us so the status of the material can be altered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That completes the evidence, Mr. Sterenberg. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the position now, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's my unhappy task to indicate that we do not have a witness to follow after this witness, and our witness will not arrive until tomorrow afternoon -- sorry, Wednesday afternoon. We have, as was indicated last week, tried to contact all the witnesses who -- that we could possibly bring, but without any success in getting a replacement for Lord Ashdown, who was dropped from this week, and also to fill the gaps that were as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's of great concern to us, Mr. Stamp, because we have tried very hard to encourage the programming of an adequate number of issues to take account of the possibility that anything can happen to any witness at any time. Expect the unexpected in this job. So the failure to have available alternatives is extremely disappointing to the Trial Chamber. It means, from what you've just said, in a week where we've especially arranged to sit for longer hours, that the loss will be over the period you've just indicated about nine and three-quarter hours of valuable court time. And we've also heard an indication that Friday may not be occupied, which would be another four hours to be added on to that, it was a shorter day. All we will do at this stage is indicate that what we do about the failure to use these hours productively will be decided in due course. It will not be decided at this stage, but it is possible that these are hours that will be allocated to the time you've been allocated to the case. We will make that decision when we feel we are fully informed -- in a fully informed position to make the decision. But you should bear it in mind as you continue to programme witnesses for 2007. Now, I take it you also want us to alter the schedule for Wednesday so that we sit in the afternoon, and that we're willing to do, but you will need to tell us what time we need to start on Wednesday because there seems to be doubt about a the time the witness will start here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we can set the time at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall adjourn now until 2.30 on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of December, 2006, at 2.30 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.20 a.m.,
